messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Kofi was a boy, he learned to read danger from ordinary sounds and smells. He grew up in a home where his father drank heavily, and some of his clearest fragments are not full scenes so much as jagged pieces: the sharp odor of alcohol on his father’s clothes, a door thrown open hard enough to strike the wall, his mother trying to move them outside toward the edge of the yard where there were trees and tall grass, as if getting into the open might calm things down. He cannot tell the story in a smooth sequence. When he tries, the details slip away from him, and what comes instead is the raw force of it in his body—sudden dread, the feeling that something terrible is about to happen—without any complete picture to match it. What remains are disconnected scraps: the slam of a door, the smell of liquor, a patch of brush and evening air. Those bits seem to have given the trauma its pathways into the present, so that even now natural spaces, the sound of doors opening or banging, and the smell of alcohol can strike him with an alarm he does not fully understand in the moment.

For most of his life, Kofi managed by staying in motion. Now 79 and still working in a warehouse, divorced and living alone, he has built his days around not being left with too much quiet. At work he lingers near the loading crew after his shift should have ended, joining in break-room talk or drifting toward any pocket of conversation rather than going straight home. He says being around people keeps his mind from “going backwards.” When a bay door crashes shut in the warehouse, or when he catches the sour smell of beer on a coworker’s breath, or when he has to walk the outside perimeter of the building past a strip of weeds and trees, the reaction in him is immediate and old. On those days he drinks more in the evening, finds reasons to call people or sit where there is noise and company, and at times picks needless arguments, especially if he feels that familiar pressure rising in his chest. Starting a quarrel gives him something concrete to focus on. It is easier, in his mind, to be angry at someone in front of him than to sit with a fear that arrives without a full memory attached.

Over the years those habits have not quieted the past so much as thickened it. Kofi describes that the more he drinks and the more he keeps himself surrounded by people or stirred up in conflict, the less able he is to deliberately remember what happened as a child. He has the sense that the memory breaks apart further when he pushes it away in these ways. He can still be flooded by the emotional force of it, but the event itself remains inaccessible, in pieces that do not join. That leaves him vulnerable to being caught off guard by triggers because they seem to come from nowhere; a slammed warehouse door or the smell of alcohol can hit him before he has words for why. In this way, his attempts to manage the distress have also helped preserve the strange, ungraspable quality of the memory.

The pattern has narrowed his life. Kofi avoids being by himself for long stretches, not out of sociability exactly, but because solitude makes room for the sensations he cannot place. He stays late around other workers, calls acquaintances just to hear another voice, and if an evening begins to feel too still, he may drink or stir tension with someone close by. Yet those same choices leave him more on edge. After nights of drinking or days marked by arguments, he notices he is jumpier the next morning at work, more likely to flinch when the heavy doors roll open or slam shut, more reactive to the smell of alcohol in the locker area, more uneasy when he passes the brush at the edge of the lot. The strategies that promise relief seem to sensitize him further to the very cues that set him off.

He finally sought help after a recent incident at the warehouse, when a loading door banged unexpectedly and he found himself overcome by terror so intense that he had to sit down, though he could not have said exactly what he was remembering. Later that week he started an argument with a coworker who had been drinking after shift, then went home and drank alone until he fell asleep. That frightened him more than he likes to admit. At his age, he says, he had believed he should have outrun this long ago. Instead he has come to fear that the feeling will keep finding him in ordinary places, and that if he ever slows down enough to face what happened, there may be more there than he can bear. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to hear a door slam, smell liquor, or walk past a stand of trees without his body being pulled back into something he still cannot fully remember.
